title: English Idioms: 11 British Phrases and Their Meanings
metaDescription: Learn 11 common British English idioms with clear meanings, plus how translators handle idioms for business. Get a free translation quote from BeTranslated.
bodyHtml:
Trust us, learning English idioms is a piece of cake

May 30, 2018
Education | Good to Know | Languages

Idioms are expressions whose meaning differs from the literal meaning of the words. They confuse language learners because the words alone do not give the answer.

Many idioms are particular to a country or region, so they offer a glimpse into local culture and ways of thinking. If you are travelling to, working in or moving to the UK, learning common English idioms will help you follow everyday conversation.

Brush up on your English with these British idioms, and see why they matter to anyone who writes or translates for a British audience.

Why learn English idioms?

If you can hold your own in everyday situations, idioms are the next step towards advanced English. They help you understand songs, television programmes, newspaper headlines and the small talk at the start of a meeting.

Native English speakers from other countries benefit too. Many idioms are regional, so an American or Australian visitor may not recognise every British phrase.

Use idioms sparingly in writing. In a business email, one well-chosen phrase sounds natural, and five in a paragraph sounds forced.

Eleven British idioms to start with

Here are eleven idioms you will hear often in the UK, with their real meanings.

  1. Working your socks off: working extremely hard. No clothing is involved.
  2. It's a piece of cake: something is very easy.
  3. I'm over the moon: you are delighted.
  4. The ball's in your court: it is your turn to decide or act.
  5. You're barking up the wrong tree: you have misunderstood or are pursuing the wrong idea.
  6. Biting off more than you can chew: taking on more than you can manage.
  7. It costs an arm and a leg: it is very expensive.
  8. At the drop of a hat: instantly, without hesitation.
  9. You've missed the boat: you are too late to take advantage of an opportunity.
  10. Don't count your chickens before they hatch: do not assume a result before it happens.
  11. Spill the beans: reveal a secret.

Try using one a day for two weeks. Say it aloud, write it in a sentence and note the situation where it fits.

Check the register before you use an idiom

Idioms differ in tone. "Over the moon" is friendly and informal, while "at the drop of a hat" suits most situations. Some phrases are common in one part of the UK and unfamiliar in another.

When you meet a new idiom, note who said it, where and to whom. That context tells you whether it suits a client meeting, a text to a friend or neither.

What idioms mean for translators and businesses

Idioms rarely survive word-for-word translation. A literal version of "it's a piece of cake" does not tell a French or Spanish reader that something is easy.

A good translator replaces an idiom with an equivalent that works in the target language. Spanish speakers say something is "pan comido" (eaten bread), and French speakers say something costs "les yeux de la tête" (the eyes from the head) where English speakers say it costs an arm and a leg. For heavy rain, English uses cats and dogs, while French uses "il pleut des cordes" (it is raining ropes).

The same applies to marketing, websites and customer emails. If you are writing for the UK market, read about British English to see how vocabulary and phrasing differ from other varieties. Idioms in slogans and product copy often need adapting rather than translating, which is a core part of localisation.

Professional help with idioms and tone

At BeTranslated our professional translators are native speakers of the language they translate into. That means they recognise idioms in the source text and choose natural alternatives in the final version.

Whether you need business documents adapted for the UK or website content localised for another market, we can help. Request a free, no-obligation quote and tell us your languages.

Frequently asked questions

What are English idioms?

English idioms are fixed expressions whose meaning cannot be worked out from the individual words. "Piece of cake" means easy, not a slice of dessert. You learn them by hearing, reading and using them in context.

What are the most common British idioms?

Common British idioms include "working your socks off", "over the moon" and "at the drop of a hat". Many are used every day in conversation, work and the media. Start with a handful and add more as you hear them.

Why are idioms hard to translate?

Their meaning is figurative and tied to culture, so a literal translation usually confuses the reader. Translators look for an idiom in the target language with the same meaning, or they rewrite the idea plainly. The choice depends on tone and audience.

Should I use idioms in business writing?

Use them sparingly and only when your reader will recognise them. International readers may not know them, and translated content can lose the effect. Clear, plain wording is safer for contracts and technical documents.

How can I learn idioms faster?

Learn them in context from British television, radio, newspapers and conversation, not from lists alone. Write each one in a sentence of your own and use it within a day. Regular, short practice works better than long sessions.
